newsitem.title: POLAND: OECD urges Poland to tighten fiscal policy.
newsitem.headline: OECD urges Poland to tighten fiscal policy.

text.p: The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) joined other international institutions on Thursday in urging Poland to tighten fiscal policy to control rapid expansion of the current account gap.

It said Poland needed financial austerity more than ever after the July floods, as money spent on flood relief would boost domestic demand and fuel the trade deficit, possibly harming economic growth and creating inflationary pressure.

"For an economy that already has an imbalance between domestic demand and production..., one would suppose that the shock (of the flood) would go in the direction of widening the current account deficit, possibly slowing GDP growth," Val Koromzay, deputy head of OECD's economic department, told a news conference.
"We recommend fiscal tightening in an appropriate way to take some pressure from domestic demand," Koromzay said.

Analysts and the central bank fear that uncontrolled growth in the current account gap will lead to the same economic difficulties as recently blighted the Czech Republic, where industrial output shrank, economic growth slowed and the crown had to be devalued.

Concern has been aggravated by the recent floods, which swamped nearly 6,000 square kms in southern Poland and killed 55 people, forcing the government to increase spending and borrow funds from the central bank.
Koromzay said the government should target the smallest possible budget deficit next year to help the central bank in its efforts to cool demand through strict monetary policy.
"The deficit (target) should be as ambitious as possible," he said.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has called on the Polish government to follow the central bank's advice to cut the budget deficit to 1.5 percent of gross domestic product next year from 2.8 percent projected for this year, and balance the budget in 1999.
But the finance ministry has adopted a more modest target of 1.9 percent, saying this should be enough to curb demand.
Koromzay said the current account gap, expected to reach about five percent of GDP this year, would not be problematic if it lasted no longer than two years.

"Is the current account gap...of five percent of GDP unsustainable? No, not for a couple of years. What if it rises to seven percent in 1998? Is it a catastrophe? International experience suggests that no, but it can't stay (that high) very long."
The current account deficit increased to $2.4 billion in the first five months of 1997, against $1.35 billion for the whole of 1996, and the government says it may exceed $6 billion this year.
